questions.q: Why, according to the editorial, do actions so often bring results no one intended?
options: People know their own ambitions but overlook the outside factors that may work against them
Yes. Overestimating oneself is called man’s greatest weakness.
Events are governed by chance
Not quite. The article says: People know their own ambitions but overlook the outside factors that may work against them.
Others deliberately spoil their plans
Not quite. The article says: People know their own ambitions but overlook the outside factors that may work against them.
People do not work hard enough
Not quite. The article says: People know their own ambitions but overlook the outside factors that may work against them.
questions.rationale: “People are aware of their ambitions, but they do not take into account the external factors which may go against their plans.”

questions.article: The Galaxy Speaks About Its Great Creator
questions.q: What response does the article expect from someone who could see the whole Milky Way at once?
options: Pride in human science
Not quite. The article says: Wonder at the greatness of its Creator.
Indifference
Not quite. The article says: Wonder at the greatness of its Creator.
Wonder at the greatness of its Creator
Right. Our galaxy is itself only a small part of the universe.
Fear of being so small
Not quite. The article says: Wonder at the greatness of its Creator.
questions.rationale: “The person will only be able to exclaim in wonderment: ‘The Creator is truly great, He made such a vast universe, of which our galaxy is only a tiny part!’”

questions.article: Happiness Is a State of Mind
questions.q: The article calls the shortcomings of life “shock treatment.” What does it mean?
options: They are punishments to be endured
Not quite. The article says: They are challenges meant to bring out a person’s inner abilities.
They are challenges meant to bring out a person’s inner abilities
Yes. Taken as challenges, they make one positive.
They are accidents with no purpose
Not quite. The article says: They are challenges meant to bring out a person’s inner abilities.
They are illnesses needing a doctor
Not quite. The article says: They are challenges meant to bring out a person’s inner abilities.
questions.rationale: “Inadequacies are like shock treatment meant to unfold a person’s inner treasure… take the differences as a challenge.”

questions.q: At a funeral a man asked what kind of prayer it was. The Imam answered, “Consider it as your own funeral prayer.” What did he mean?
options: The question was improper
Not quite. The article says: The prayer is truly said by one who sees his own death in the death before him.
The prayer is truly said by one who sees his own death in the death before him
Well read. It is a reminder, not a mere ritual.
The prayer had already been said for him
Not quite. The article says: The prayer is truly said by one who sees his own death in the death before him.
The man should leave the congregation
Not quite. The article says: The prayer is truly said by one who sees his own death in the death before him.
questions.rationale: “The true funeral prayer is said by the one who sees his own death in the death of the deceased before us.”

questions.q: A cricketer said he thinks only of the ball in front of him and forgets the last one. Why does the article call this good advice for life?
options: Memory cannot be trusted
Not quite. The article says: Dwelling on the past – success or failure – divides one’s energy and harms the task ahead.
The future is always better
Not quite. The article says: Dwelling on the past – success or failure – divides one’s energy and harms the task ahead.
The past is usually unpleasant
Not quite. The article says: Dwelling on the past – success or failure – divides one’s energy and harms the task ahead.
Dwelling on the past – success or failure – divides one’s energy and harms the task ahead
Correct. Past success breeds pride; past failure, distraction.
questions.rationale: “If you remember the past, your energy will be divided into focussing on two phases of life… A wise person is one who completely forgets the past and focusses totally on the future.”

questions.q: A visitor asked to call on a statesman who had died years before. What does the article take from the story?
options: News travels slowly between countries
Not quite. The article says: Not everything can be spelt out; without some prior knowledge a person cannot grasp what he is told.
It is rude to ask questions abroad
Not quite. The article says: Not everything can be spelt out; without some prior knowledge a person cannot grasp what he is told.
Not everything can be spelt out; without some prior knowledge a person cannot grasp what he is told
Yes. One must already know “half.”
Officials should brief travellers more fully
Not quite. The article says: Not everything can be spelt out; without some prior knowledge a person cannot grasp what he is told.
questions.rationale: “Everything cannot be spelt out in words; there are some things that one has to know oneself… if one does not have half of it in one’s mind beforehand, then how can one grasp the whole picture?”

questions.q: What “law of nature” does the article mention about someone who loses a faculty such as sight?
options: The person must depend wholly on others
Not quite. The article says: New capacities awaken in compensation, if the loss is taken with patience.
The loss can always be reversed
Not quite. The article says: New capacities awaken in compensation, if the loss is taken with patience.
New capacities awaken in compensation, if the loss is taken with patience
Right. Hence “differently-abled.”
The other senses weaken as well
Not quite. The article says: New capacities awaken in compensation, if the loss is taken with patience.
questions.rationale: “If someone loses one part of his body, he develops new capacities in compensation… such a person takes his loss of vision in a positive sense, as a result of which his intellectual capacities are awakened.”

questions.q: With what does the article identify religious extremism?
options: Deep personal devotion
Not quite. The article says: Religiosity reduced to outward form, once the inner spirit has been lost.
Religiosity reduced to outward form, once the inner spirit has been lost
Yes. It arises in a community’s decline.
Excessive charity
Not quite. The article says: Religiosity reduced to outward form, once the inner spirit has been lost.
Too much study of scripture
Not quite. The article says: Religiosity reduced to outward form, once the inner spirit has been lost.
questions.rationale: “Religious extremism is but another name for religiosity based simply on form.”

questions.q: Where, says the article, must the renewal of such a community begin?
options: With a new government
Not quite. The article says: With the reform of individual members.
With the reform of individual members
Exactly. Institutions built by unreformed people only look grand.
With larger organisations
Not quite. The article says: With the reform of individual members.
With grander buildings
Not quite. The article says: With the reform of individual members.
questions.rationale: “Efforts to work with a community that has degenerated have to begin with the reform of individual members, and not in the form of collective efforts.”

questions.q: A young cricketer died after being struck in a match. What message does the article say every death carries for the living?
options: That the young should not make plans
Not quite. The article says: That their own chance still remains and should be used.
That sport is too dangerous
Not quite. The article says: That their own chance still remains and should be used.
That their own chance still remains and should be used
Well read. No death is “untimely” in God’s plan.
That life is unfair
Not quite. The article says: That their own chance still remains and should be used.
questions.rationale: “For those who are alive, every death gives a message that they still have their chance and therefore must avail of it.”
